title: What is the oldest book in the world?
subtitle: Circa 2000 BC
subject: litterature
description: Some 4,000 years ago in Mesopotamia, the story of a tyrannical king who learned wisdom was pressed into clay. Two-thirds of the text have reached us, and the rest is still being sought.
author: simon-lea

hero.hook: The oldest book in the world has no pages: it is written in clay, and a third of it is still missing.

blocks.text: The oldest book in the world is not a bound book. It is a long poem, the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, written some **4,000 years** ago in [[Mesopotamia]], in modern-day Iraq. Its hero, **Gilgamesh**, is the tyrannical king of the city of [[Uruk]]. The text calls him, rather confusingly, "two-thirds divine and one-third human."

As punishment for his cruelty, the mother goddess creates [[Enkidu]], a wild man sent to fight him and humble him. But a dream warns the king that Enkidu will become his friend. A sacred prostitute, Shamhat, tames him in seven days and nights. The two men fight, then become inseparable, and possibly lovers. Their friendship leads to adventure, then to grief, then to the quest for immortality.

Little is known about the origins of the poem. Archaeology confirms its age: around **4,000 years**. We have roughly **two-thirds** of it, preserved on the original clay tablets, written in [[cuneiform]] script. Fortunately for us, clay is extremely durable.

blocks.caption: Tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh in cuneiform, found at Nineveh (British Museum).

blocks.text: New tablets keep coming out of the ground, and the hope is that the missing third will one day be found. Like every text this old, it blends legends older than itself with much later additions: some passages may date from **a thousand years** after the original. The meaning of the poem therefore shifts depending on which version you read.

Despite these borrowings and touch-ups, experts are fairly confident that the *Epic of Gilgamesh* has one consistent author. We also know that a real King Gilgamesh once existed, although the king in the poem has been greatly mythologized. Other kings of mythology, King Midas for example, met the same fate.

Studies of the oldest tablets show that the original story was concerned above all with King Gilgamesh, his life and his adventures. But once the later additions are taken into account, the poem becomes something else entirely: a reflection on human mortality and on the meaning of life and death.

sections.title: Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven

blocks.text: On their adventures together, Gilgamesh and Enkidu battle monsters. The first is [[Humbaba]], an ogre who guards the Cedar Forest, a legendary place where kings went to get timber for their buildings. Humbaba is killed and the trees are felled. The killing, followed by this vandalism, enrages the gods.

After the battle, as Gilgamesh is washing himself, the goddess [[Ishtar]] sees him and offers him her love. The king knows her reputation: none of her lovers has lived long. He refuses, rudely. Enraged, Ishtar unleashes the Bull of Heaven on him. The two friends kill it, and Enkidu hurls one of its hind legs at the goddess. These feats show Gilgamesh's strength, but also a hubris the gods will not leave unpunished.
The constellation Taurus shows a bull without hindquarters. Some see in it a memory of Enkidu tearing off a hind leg of the Bull of Heaven to throw at Ishtar.

As punishment for the death of the Bull of Heaven, the gods condemn Enkidu to die. The loss of his friend makes Gilgamesh aware of his own mortality. He begins to fear death and sets out to find the secret of immortality. Only one man is known to have beaten death: [[Utnapishtim]].

blocks.caption: The "Flood Tablet," the eleventh tablet of the epic, which tells the story of Utnapishtim (British Museum).

blocks.text: His story predates Noah's, and is almost identical: after surviving the flood, he and his wife became immortal. When Gilgamesh finally meets him, Utnapishtim advises him to give up his quest for eternal life. He does give him a plant that restores youth. A snake steals it.

Noah and Utnapishtim are both forewarned of the flood and told to build an enormous boat to shelter the animals. When the tablets were first translated, finding this story thousands of years before Genesis shook the world: proof to some that the story of Noah was borrowed from an older religion, confirmation to others that a great flood had really happened.

Gilgamesh gives up on immortality and goes home to Uruk, to a life of quiet contemplation. The lesson of the oldest book in the world seems to fit in one sentence: accept that life is fleeting, and prefer wisdom to action.
The *Epic of Gilgamesh*, pressed into clay 4,000 years ago and still incomplete, went from a tale of royal adventures to a meditation on death over a thousand years of additions.

sources.text: B. B. Powell, Classical Myth, 9th ed., Oxford University Press, New York, 2020, p. 326.
